Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Robert had always prided himself on his composure, a necessary trait for a foreign correspondent covering some of the world’s most volatile regions. That composure shattered three years ago when he was taken captive during an assignment in a remote area. For weeks, he endured the suffocating darkness of a windowless room, often blindfolded, his hands bound tightly behind his back. His captors were unpredictable, their presence often announced by the cloying, sickly sweet smell of cheap alcohol that permeated the small space. They would grab him roughly by the neck and shoulders during interrogations, forcing his head down, or pushing him against the wall, leaving a persistent ache that radiated through his upper spine. Every sudden movement, every harsh voice, every unexpected sound was a jolt of terror, a constant reminder of his utter helplessness.

Now, back in his quiet suburban home, the world felt both too calm and perpetually threatening. A sudden sharp pain in his neck, perhaps from sleeping awkwardly, could instantly transport Robert back to the grimy floor of that room, the phantom pressure of a captor’s hand on his nape. When his wife, Sarah, would reach out to touch his arm in a gesture of affection or concern, he would flinch, his muscles tensing, a wave of profound unease washing over him. The intimacy of physical contact had become fraught with the memory of violation. Even a casual stroll through a supermarket could become an ordeal; if he caught a whiff of alcohol from a spilled bottle or a passing shopper, a cold dread would seize him, his heart hammering against his ribs as if his captors were once again just out of sight.

The memories themselves were relentless. When they struck, it was not merely a thought, but a vivid, horrifying film that played over and over in his mind, often without warning. He could be reviewing an article for submission, or simply trying to read a book, when the scene would force its way in: the faces of his captors, the texture of the rough burlap sack over his head, the taste of dust and fear. Each time, the terror he had felt in that room, a primal, bone-deep fear, would surge through his body, leaving him breathless and trembling, drenched in a cold sweat. He would try to push it away, to focus on the present, but the loop would continue, an unwelcome, vivid replay of his worst nightmare.

His professional life as a journalist had become a minefield. Sitting in the newsroom, the clatter of keyboards, the sudden ring of a phone, or a colleague’s unexpected laugh would make him jump, his entire body going rigid. He was on high alert for any unexpected or loud sounds, his senses constantly scanning, interpreting innocuous office noises as potential threats. He found himself perpetually watchful, hyperalert to his surroundings, as if danger lurked just beyond the periphery of his vision. This constant vigilance meant he often reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong, a sharp retort to a harmless question, a sudden movement away from a friendly colleague. He had stopped volunteering for field assignments, preferring the controlled environment of the office, but even there, the perceived threats were numerous.

Over the months, this persistent state of alarm had taken a toll on his marriage. Sarah, though understanding, felt increasingly distant from him. His aversion to touch, his frequent irritability, and his preoccupation with an invisible threat had created a chasm between them. He found himself retreating, spending more time in his study, ostensibly working, but often simply staring blankly at his screen, waiting for the next memory to intrude or the next perceived threat to materialize. The cumulative weight of these experiences had become unbearable, pushing him to a breaking point where the only path forward, he believed, was to seek help before he lost everything that remained.
